items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon and Module Wrap-Up (CER) Encounter the Phenomenon: Why do all tropical cyclones in the southern hemisphere rotate the same direction?

body.html: Air flows toward a low-pressure center. We want the rotation direction in the southern <sub>hemisphere and the reason.</sub>

Earth is a rotating frame of reference, so moving air seems to be pushed sideways by the Coriolis "force." In the <sub>southern hemisphere the deflection is to the left of the direction of motion. This is not a real force. An observer in space sees the</sub> <sub>air move straight while the ground turns underneath it.</sub>

<sub>Air south of a low moves north toward it. It is deflected to its left, which is west of the low.</sub> <sub>Air north of a low moves south toward it and is deflected to its left, which is east of the low.</sub> <sub>Air east of the low moves west and is deflected south. Air west of the low moves east and is deflected north.</sub> <sub>Deflected to the left everywhere, the air circles the low clockwise (west on the south side, east on the north side).</sub>

answer.html: Claim: every southern-hemisphere cyclone spins clockwise. Evidence: the Coriolis <sub>"force" deflects any horizontally moving object to its left in the southern hemisphere, and satellite pictures of cyclones such as</sub> <sub>those in the Indian Ocean show clockwise spiral cloud bands. </sub><sub>Reasoning:</sub><sub> inflowing air toward a low is always deflected to the</sub> <sub>left, and that makes a clockwise circulation. In the northern hemisphere the deflection is to the right, so storms there rotate</sub> <sub>counterclockwise.</sub>

check.html: Reversing the rule gives counterclockwise rotation in the north, which matches observation.

items.title: Module Wrap-Up: Revisit the Phenomenon / Explain Your Reasoning

body.html: The final CER uses the same reasoning, now supported by evidence from each lesson.

ork</sub><sub>: Lesson 1 gives the language of rotation (</sub>𝜃<sub>, </sub>𝜔<sub>, </sub>𝛼<sub>). Earth turns once per day,</sub> 𝜔= 2𝜋/ (86 400 s) = 7.27 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> rad/s<sub>. Lesson 2 shows a net torque is needed to change rotation. Lesson 3 explains</sub> <sub>that Earth is a rotating frame. Points near the equator move east faster than points near the poles. For example, with an</sub> <sub>equatorial speed of 464 m/s, the ground speed at 20° S latitude is </sub>464cos20° = 436<sub> m/s, while at 50° S it is</sub> 464cos50° = 298<sub> m/s. Air moving south from 20° S keeps its 436 m/s eastward speed, so it runs ahead (east) of the slower</sub> <sub>ground. Moving south, east is to the left.</sub>

answer.html: The evidence (Earth's rotation, the leftward Coriolis deflection in the southern hemisphere, and low-pressure inflow) <sub>supports the claim that southern-hemisphere cyclones rotate clockwise. If you wrote a different claim, revise it to this one.</sub>

check.html: The claim predicts the opposite spin in the northern hemisphere, and observations agree. <sub>Not solvable from the text:</sub><sub> the "STEM Unit Project" revisit refers to a project you built earlier in your own course. A sample revisit: if</sub> <sub>your project used a spinning or balancing device, state one place where torque or moment of inertia mattered, and explain how the</sub> <sub>module's equations (</sub>𝜏= 𝐹𝑟sin𝜃<sub>, </sub>𝛼= 𝜏/ 𝐼<sub>) would improve your design.</sub>

items.title: Get It? Compare the angular velocity and angular acceleration of a rotating body

body.html: A playground carousel is at rest, then pushed, then allowed to coast. Compare ω and α in each <sub>stage.</sub>

Angular velocity ω is how fast the angle changes (rad/s). Angular acceleration α is how fast ω itself changes <sub>(rad/s²). While being pushed from rest, ω grows from zero, so α is positive (ω is small but α is not zero). While coasting at</sub> <sub>constant ω, α is zero even though ω is large. Friction then slowly brings it to rest, so α is opposite to ω.</sub>

answer.html: ω = Δθ/Δt measures how fast the carousel turns; α = Δω/Δt measures how fast that rate changes. Their units are rad/s <sub>and rad/s². A carousel can have large ω with α = 0 (steady coasting), or α ≠ 0 with ω = 0 for an instant (just starting to move).</sub>

items.title: Focus Question: How would you describe the rotation of a hurricane?

body.html: Use the quantities of the lesson: angular displacement θ, angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt, and angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt, with counterclockwise positive.

A northern-hemisphere hurricane turns counterclockwise, so its θ and ω are positive. Each parcel of air at radius r moves at v = rω, so the winds are fastest where ω r is largest. Unlike a rigid body, a hurricane's different parts do not all share the same ω (the eye turns slowly, the eyewall fast). If the storm strengthens, ω increases and α is positive.

answer.html: A hurricane is described by a positive (counterclockwise, northern hemisphere) angular velocity ω in rad/s, with linear wind speed v = rω at radius r. It is not a rigid body, so ω varies with distance from the center.

check.html: Units rad/s and m/s agree with the book's definitions.

body.html: A watch hand is a rigid body, so all its points sweep the same angle Δθ. A point at radius r travels x = rΔθ.

Every point on the hand turns through the same angle in the same time. But points farther from the center have a larger r, so the arc length x = rΔθ is larger. The tip travels farthest; a point near the pivot barely moves.

answer.html: Yes, all parts have the same angular displacement. No, they do not move the same linear distance: 𝑥= 𝑟𝛥𝜃 grows with the distance from the axis.
